title.en: Horus of Behutet and the Winged Disk
title.zh: 貝胡特特荷魯斯與雙翼日盤

region.en: Edfu (Behutet), Upper Egypt (temple of Horus, where the legend is inscribed)
region.zh: 埃及上埃及埃德富（貝胡特特，荷魯斯神廟刻壁處）

texts.period: Inscribed at Edfu in the Ptolemaic temple; text purports to date from the 363rd year of Ra-Heru-Khuti (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), ch. IV, 'The Legend of Horus of Behutet and the Winged Disk'

summary.en: The founding myth of Egypt's most famous temple sign: Horus of Behutet flies into the horizon as the great Winged Disk and annihilates the rebels of Ra — followers turned crocodiles and hippopotami, slain by the hundreds before Edfu — until Set himself is captured, beheaded, and dragged through his own district; Thoth orders the Winged Disk placed above every temple in the land.
summary.zh: 埃及最著名神廟紋章之緣起：貝胡特特荷魯斯化為雙翼日盤翱翔天際，誅殺謀逆之眾——敵者化鱷與河馬，於埃德富城前被逐一誅戮——直至塞特被縛、斬首、以其矛貫首拖行己土；托特遂命日盤置於全國諸神廟之上。

sensitivity.note: Ancient temple foundation legend; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: And Heru-Behutet flew up into the horizon in the form of the great Winged Disk, for which reason he is called 'Great god, lord of heaven,' unto this day. And when he saw the enemies in the heights of heaven he set out to follow after them in the form of the great Winged Disk, and he attacked with such terrific force those who opposed him, that they could neither see with their eyes nor hear with their ears, and each of them slew his fellow. In a moment of time there was not a single creature left alive. Then Heru Behutet, shining with very many colours, came in the form of the great Winged Disk to the Boat of Ra-Harmachis, and Thoth said unto Ra, 'O Lord of the gods, Behutet hath returned in the form of the great Winged Disk, shining [with many colours] . . . . . . children;' for this reason he is called Heru-Behutet unto this day.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), the Winged Disk legend, section XIII.

passages.text: And behold the enemies [of Ra] rushed into the water, and they took the forms of [crocodiles and] hippopotami, but nevertheless Ra-Heru-Khuti sailed over the waters in his boat, and when the crocodiles and the hippopotami had come nigh unto him, they opened wide their jaws in order to destroy Ra-Heru-Khuti. And when Heru-Behutet arrived and his followers who were behind him in the forms of workers in metal, each having in his hands an iron spear and a chain, according to his name, they smote the crocodiles and the hippopotami; and there were brought in there straightway six hundred and fifty-one crocodiles, which had been slain before the city of Edfu.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), section XIII.

passages.text: Then Set rose up and came forth, and raged loudly with words of cursing and abuse because of the things which Heru-behutet had done in respect of the slaughter of the enemies. And Ra said unto Thoth, 'This fiend Nehaha-hra uttereth words at the top of his voice because of the things which Heru-Behutet hath done unto him;' and Thoth said unto Ra, 'Cries of this kind shall be called Nehaha-hra unto this day.' And Heru-Behutet did battle with the Enemy for a period of time, and he hurled his iron lance at him, and he threw him down on the ground in this region, which is called Pa-Rerehtu unto this day. Then Heru-Behutet came and brought the Enemy with him, and his spear was in his neck, and his chain was round his hands and arms, and the weapon of Horus had fallen on his mouth and had closed it; and he went with him before his father Ra, who said, 'O Horus, thou Winged Disk, twice great (Urui-Tenten) is the deed of valour which thou hast done, and thou hast cleansed the district.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), section XV.

passages.text: Then Horus the son of Isis cut off the head of the Enemy [Set], and the heads of his fiends in the presence of father Ra and of the great company of the gods, and he dragged him by his feet through his district with his spear driven through his head and back. And Ra said unto Thoth, 'Let the son of Osiris drag the being of disaster through his territory;' and Thoth said, 'It shall be called Ateh,' and this hath been the name of the region from that day to this. And Isis, the divine lady, spake before Ra, saying, 'Let the exalted Winged Disk become the amulet of my son Horus, who hath cut off the head of the Enemy and the heads of his fiends.' — Then Thoth made the image of the Winged Disk to be in every sanctuary and in every temple, where they now are, wherein are all the gods and all the goddesses from this day onwards.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), sections XV and XIX.

title.en: Isis the Kite: The Origin of Horus in the Marshes
title.zh: 鳶形伊西斯：荷魯斯之誕生

region.en: Chemmis marshes, Delta, Egypt (the hidden nest of Horus)
region.zh: 埃及三角洲克米斯沼澤（荷魯斯隱巢）

texts.period: Hymn of the New Kingdom or later (Budge translation 1912); the doctrine goes back to the Pyramid Texts

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), 'A Hymn to Osiris and a Legend of the Origin of Horus'

summary.en: From the great Hymn to Osiris: Isis flies as a kite across the land crying her death-wails until she finds her murdered brother; with feathered light and the air of her wings she revives him, draws out his essence, and makes from it an heir — Horus — whom she suckles in solitude where none knows his place, until the gods gather to bestow on him the rank that is his by right.
summary.zh: 《奧西里斯頌》所載：伊西斯化為鳶鳥環飛大地、哀哭尋兄；以羽光與雙翼之氣使兄復甦，取其精而生嗣子荷魯斯；獨居荒沼哺育幼神，無人知其所在——至諸神齊集，方以固有之尊位歸還於他。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn material; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Thou settest [thy] son upon the great throne of his father Keb. Thou art the beloved one of thy mother Nut, whose valour is most mighty [when] thou overthrowest the Seba Fiend. Thou hast slaughtered thy enemy, and hast put the fear of thee into thy Adversary. Thou art the bringer in of the remotest boundaries, and art stable of heart, and thy two feet are lifted up; thou art the heir of Keb and of the sovereignty of the Two Lands, and he (i.e. Keb) hath seen thy splendid qualities, and hath commanded thee to guide the lands (i.e., the world) by thy hand so long as times [and seasons] endure.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), the Hymn to Osiris — the inheritance of Geb's throne.

passages.text: Thy sister [Isis] acted as a protectress to thee. She drove [thy] enemies away, she averted seasons [of calamity from thee], she recited the word (or, formula) with the magical power of her mouth, [being] skilled of tongue and never halting for a word, being perfect in command and word. Isis the magician avenged her brother. She went about seeking for him untiringly. She flew round and round over this earth uttering wailing cries of grief, and she did not alight on the ground until she had found him. She made light [to come forth] from her feathers, she made air to come into being by means of her two wings, and she cried out the death cries for her brother.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), the Hymn to Osiris — Isis the kite.

passages.text: She made to rise up the helpless members of him whose heart was at rest, she drew from him his essence, and she made therefrom an heir. She suckled the child in solitariness and none knew where his place was, and he grew in strength. His hand is mighty (or, victorious) within the house of Keb, and the Company of the Gods rejoice greatly at the coming of Horus, the son of Osiris, whose heart is firmly stablished, the triumphant one, the son of Isis, the flesh and bone of Osiris.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), the Hymn to Osiris — the conception and hiding of Horus.

passages.text: The Tchatcha of Truth, and the Company of the Gods, and Neb-er-tcher himself, and the Lords of Truth, gather together to him, and assemble therein. Verily those who defeat iniquity rejoice in the House of Keb to bestow the divine rank and dignity upon him to whom it belongeth, and the sovereignty upon him whose it is by right.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), the Hymn to Osiris — the vindication of Horus.

title.en: The Great Hymn to Osiris, Lord of Eternity
title.zh: 奧西里斯大頌，永恆之主

region.en: Abydos, Upper Egypt (Osiris' principal cult center, named throughout the hymn)
region.zh: 埃及上埃及阿拜多斯（頌中反覆稱名之主祭中心）

texts.period: New Kingdom hymn (Budge translation 1912); recited in the Osiris temples of the Two Lands

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), 'A Hymn to Osiris and a Legend of the Origin of Horus' (opening sections)

summary.en: The great liturgical hymn of the Osiris cult: the god is addressed by his names at every city — Busiris, Heliopolis, Memphis, Herakleopolis, Abydos — as Lord of eternity whose transformations are sublime, whose gates of heaven open at his word, and whose son Horus sits established on his throne.
summary.zh: 奧西里斯祭團大頌：神以各城之名受拜——布西里斯、赫利奧波利斯、孟菲斯、赫拉克利奧波利斯、阿拜多斯——尊號連綿，變化無方；天門聞其言而啟，其子荷魯斯已定於其座。

sensitivity.note: Ancient temple hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Homage to thee, Osiris, Lord of eternity, King of the gods, whose names are manifold, whose transformations are sublime, whose form is hidden in the temples, whose Ka is holy, the Governor of Tetut, the mighty one of possessions in the shrine, the Lord of praises in the nome of Anetch, President of the tchefa food in Anu, Lord who art commemorated in [the town of] Maati, the mysterious (or, hidden) Soul, the Lord of Qerret, the sublime one in White Wall, the Soul of Ra [and] his very body, who hast thy dwelling in Henensu, the beneficent one, who art praised in Nart, [who inspirest] great terror in Shas-hetep, Lord of eternity, Governor of Abtu (Abydos).
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), the Hymn to Osiris, opening address.

passages.text: Thy seat (or, domain) reacheth far into Ta-tchesert, and thy name is firmly stablished in the mouth[s] of men. Thou art the two-fold substance of the Two Lands everywhere, and the divine food (tchef) of the Kau, the Governor of the Companies of the Gods, and the beneficent (or, perfect) Spirit-soul among Spirit-souls. The god Nu draweth his waters from thee, and thou bringest forth the north wind at eventide, and wind from thy nostrils to the satisfaction of thy heart. Thy heart flourisheth, and thou bringest forth the splendour of tchef food.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), the Hymn to Osiris.

passages.text: The height of heaven and the stars [thereof] are obedient unto thee, and thou makest to be opened the great gates [of the sky]. Thou art the lord to whom praises are sung in the southern heaven, thou art he to whom thanks are given in the northern heaven. The stars which never diminish are under the place of thy face, and thy seats are the stars which never rest. Offerings appear before thee by the command of Keb. The Companies of the Gods ascribe praise unto thee, the Star-gods of the Tuat smell the earth before thee, the domains [make] bowings [before thee], and the ends of the earth make supplication to thee [when] they see thee.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), the Hymn to Osiris.

passages.text: Thou rollest up into the horizon, thou settest the light above the darkness, thou illuminest [the Two Lands] with the light from thy two plumes, thou floodest the Two Lands like the Disk at the beginning of the dawn. Thy White Crown pierceth the height of heaven saluting the stars, thou art the guide of every god. Thou art perfect in command and word. Thou art the favoured one of the Great Company of the Gods, and thou art the beloved one of the Little Company of the Gods.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), the Hymn to Osiris.

title.en: The Death and Resurrection of Horus: Isis and the Seven Scorpions
title.zh: 荷魯斯之死與復活：伊西斯與七蠍

region.en: Chemmis marshes and Pa-Sui, Delta, Egypt (Isis' flight with the child Horus)
region.zh: 埃及三角洲克米斯沼澤與帕-蘇伊（伊西斯攜子逃亡地）

texts.period: Metternich Stele cycle, 30th Dynasty-Saite (c. 380-570 BCE); the cippus spells are older (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), ch. VIII, 'The Legend of the Death of Horus through the Sting of a Scorpion' and the Narrative of Isis

summary.en: Fleeing Set with the child Horus, Isis is escorted by seven scorpions; a rich woman who shuts her door against the goddess pays when her own son is stung, while Horus too is struck down and lies dead in the marshes. Isis' cry stops the Boat of Ra itself, and Thoth descends with the spells of maa-kheru to drive out the poison — the mythic warrant of Egypt's healing cippi, 'for him that is under the knife.'
summary.zh: 伊西斯攜幼荷魯斯避塞特之追，七蠍相隨；拒她入門的富家婦人其子遭螫，而小荷魯斯亦中蠍毒倒斃沼澤。伊西斯之哭喊令拉之舟停駛，托特攜『真言之威』降臨驅毒——此即埃及療病石碑之神話依據，『為刀下之人』而誦。

sensitivity.note: Ancient healing-stele cycle; no living community restrictions. The myth legitimized magical medicine (cippi of Horus), quoted here for comparative scholarship only.

passages.text: I came forth [from the dwelling] at the time of evening, and there came forth the Seven Scorpions which were to accompany me and to strike for me with [their] stings. Two scorpions, Tefen and Befen, were behind me, two scorpions, Mestet and Mestetef, were by my side, and three scorpions, Petet, Thetet, and Maatet (or, Martet), were for preparing the road for me. I charged them very strictly, and my words penetrated into their ears: 'Have no knowledge of [any], make no cry to the Tesheru beings, and pay no attention to the son of a man who belongeth to a man of no account.' So the guardian of the company brought me to the boundaries of the city of Pa-Sui.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), the Narrative of Isis, section I.

passages.text: When I had arrived at the place where the people lived I came to the houses wherein dwelt the wives [and] husbands. And a certain woman of quality spied me as I was journeying along the road, and she shut her doors on me. Now she was sick at heart by reason of those [scorpions] which were with me. Then [the Seven Scorpions] took counsel concerning her, and they all at one time shot out their venom on the tail of the scorpion Tefen; as for me, the woman Taha opened her door, and I entered into the house of the miserable lady. Then the scorpion Tefen entered in under the leaves of the door and smote (i.e., stung) the son of Usert, and a fire broke out in the house of Usert, and there was no water there to extinguish it; [but] the sky rained upon the house of Usert, though it was not the season for rain.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Narrative of Isis.

passages.text: I went away to the city of Am, [where] the people gave thanks [for me] through [their] fear of my making trouble [for them]. I passed the day in seeking to provide food for the child, [and] on returning to take Horus into my arms I found him, Horus, the beautiful one of gold, the boy, the child, without [life]. He had bedewed the ground with the water of his eye, and with foam from his lips. His body was motionless, his heart was powerless to move, and the sinews (or, muscles) of his members were [helpless]. I sent forth a cry, [saying]: 'I, even I, lack a son to make answer [for me]. [My] two breasts are full to overflowing, [but] my body is empty. My father is in the Tuat, my mother is in Aqert, and my elder brother is in the sarcophagus.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Narrative of Isis, section 101 — the dead child Horus.

passages.text: And Isis sent forth her voice into heaven, and made supplication to the Boat of Millions of Years, and the Disk stopped in its journeying, and moved not from the place whereon it rested. Then came forth Thoth, who is equipped with his spells (or, words of power), and possesseth the great word of command of maa-kheru, [and said:] 'Fear not, fear not, O goddess Isis, fear not, fear not, O Nephthys, and let not anxiety [be to you]. I have come from heaven having life to heal(?) the child for his mother. Horus is protected as the Dweller in his Disk, who lighteth up the Two Lands by the splendour of his two Eyes; and he who is under the knife is likewise protected.' — [And Thoth said:] 'Wake up, Horus! Thy protection is established. Make thou happy the heart of thy mother Isis.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Narrative of Isis — the resurrection of Horus by Thoth.

title.en: Khnum and the Seven Years' Famine

region.en: Elephantine (Abu), First Cataract, Egypt (temple and quarries of Khnum)
region.zh: 埃及第一瀑布象島（庫努姆神廟與採石場）

texts.period: Stele text set in reign of Djoser (3rd Dynasty, c. 2670 BCE), carved in Ptolemaic times at Philae/Sahal (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), ch. VII, 'The Legend of Khnemu and a Seven Years' Famine'

summary.en: For seven years the Nile has failed and Egypt starves; King Tcheser (Djoser) sends his governor to the House of Life to find the river's birthplace, and learns that all waters come from the two caverns at Elephantine where Khnum dwells. In a dream the potter-god reminds the king who fashioned his body, then promises an eternal flood — and the king, waking, decrees the temple's tithe-endowment carved in stone forever.
summary.zh: 尼羅七年不漲，埃及大饑；王捷塞爾遣官往生命之屋查河源，得知諸水皆出象島雙穴，庫努姆居焉。陶匠之神夢中告王：『我造爾身』，許以永不匱乏之洪——王醒後刻石頒詔，永賦神廟什一之稅。

sensitivity.note: Late-period stele legend set in Old Kingdom; no living community restrictions. Coordinates at Elephantine (modern Aswan area) since the myth is anchored to the island's temple and quarries.

passages.text: Misery hath laid hold upon me [as I sit] upon the great throne by reason of those who dwell in the Great House. My heart is grievously afflicted by reason of the exceedingly great evil [which hath happened] because Hapi (i.e., the Nile) hath not come forth in my time to the [proper] height for seven years. Grain is very scarce, vegetables are lacking altogether, every kind of thing which men eat for their food hath ceased, and every man [now] plundereth his neighbour. Men wish to walk, but are unable to move, the child waileth, the young man draggeth his limbs along, and the hearts of the aged folk are crushed with despair.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), the Famine Stele, the king's despatch.

passages.text: He said unto me: 'There is a city in the middle of the stream wherefrom Hapi maketh his appearance; Abu was its name in the beginning; it is the City of the Beginning, and it is the Nome of the City of the Beginning. [It reacheth] to Uaua, which is the beginning of the land. There is too a flight of steps, which reareth itself to a great height, and is the support of Ra, when he maketh his calculation to prolong life to everyone; Netchemtchem Ankh is the name of its abode. The two Qerti is the name of the water, and they are the two breasts from which every good thing cometh forth.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), the Famine Stele — the revelation of the Nile's birthplace.

passages.text: He openeth his eyes, and his heart was inclined [to hear] me, and his words were strong [when he said], 'I am Khnemu, who fashioned thee. My two hands were about thee and knitted together thy body, and made healthy thy members; and it is I who gave thee thy heart. Yet the minerals (or, precious stones) [lie] under each other, [and they have done so] from olden time, and no man hath worked them in order to build the houses of the god, or to restore those which have fallen into ruin, or to hew out shrines for the gods of the South and of the North, or to do what he ought to do for his lord, notwithstanding that I am the Lord and the Creator.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), the Famine Stele — Khnum's rebuke.

passages.text: I am [he] who created himself, Nu, the Great [God], who came into being at the beginning, [and] Hapi, who riseth according to his will, in order to give health to him that laboureth for me. I am the Director and Guide of all men at their seasons, the Most Great, the Father of the Gods, Shu, the Great One, the Chief of the Earth. A lake of water hath been poured out for me, [namely,] Hap (i.e., the Nile), which embraceth the field-land, and his embrace provideth the [means of] life for every one. I will make Hap (i.e., the Nile) rise for thee, and [in] no year shall [he] fail, and he shall spread himself out in rest upon every land. Green plants and herbs and trees shall bow beneath [the weight of] their produce. Misery shall pass away, and the emptiness of their store-houses of grain shall come to an end.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), the Famine Stele — Khnum's promise.

title.en: Khonsu and the Princess of Bekhten

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (temple of Khonsu at Karnak, where the Bentresh stele stood)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（卡納克孔蘇神廟，本特雷什碑立處）

texts.period: Bentresh Stele, 3rd Intermediate or early Late Period, set in year 33 of Ramesses II (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), ch. VI, 'A Legend of Khensu Nefer-hetep and the Princess of Bekhten'

summary.en: The Pharaoh marries the daughter of the Prince of Bekhten, but her sister falls possessed by a spirit no scribe can cure. Twice the god Khonsu is petitioned; his statue, given the elder god's protective power 'in a fourfold measure,' sails a year and five months to Bekhten, defeats the spirit in open conversation, and stays three years and nine months — until the god flies home as a golden hawk in the prince's dream.
summary.zh: 法老娶貝克滕王之女，其妹卻為邪靈所附，書吏莫能治。神孔蘇兩度受請；其像承長神護力『四倍』，舟行一年五月抵貝克滕，當眾折服邪靈，留三年九月——至王夢中化金鷹飛歸埃及。

sensitivity.note: Ancient healing-provenance stele; no living community restrictions. 'miraculous-birth' tag used here for the marvel-hagiography genre (healing miracle), the closest index category; recorded as an interpretive choice.

passages.text: And the Prince of Bekhten [also] caused his gifts to be brought, and he set his eldest daughter at the head of them all, and he addressed words of praise to His Majesty, and prayed to him for his life. And the maiden was beautiful, and His Majesty considered her to be the most lovely [woman] in the world, and he wrote down as her title, 'Great Royal Wife, Ra-neferu'; and when His Majesty arrived in Egypt, he did for her whatsoever was done for the Royal Wife.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), the Bekhten legend.

passages.text: He spake words of adoration to His Majesty, saying, 'I have come unto thee, my King and Lord, on behalf of Bent-Resht, the younger sister of the Royal Wife Ra-neferu. [Some] disease hath penetrated into her members, and I beseech Thy Majesty to send a man of learning to see her.' And when the man of learning had arrived in Bekhten, he found Bent-Resht in the condition of a woman who is possessed by a spirit, and he found this spirit to be an evil one, and to be hostile in his disposition towards him. And the Prince of Bekhten sent a messenger a second time into the presence of His Majesty, saying, 'O King, my Lord, I pray His (i.e., Thy) Majesty to command that a god be brought hither to contend against the spirit.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), the Bekhten legend.

passages.text: And Khensu in Thebes, [called] 'Nefer-Hetep,' inclined his head with a deep inclination twice. And he made [his] protective power to pass into Khensu, [called] 'Pa-ari-sekher-em-Uast,' in a fourfold measure. Then His Majesty commanded that Khensu, [called] 'Pa-ari-sekher-em-Uast,' should set out on his journey in a great boat, [accompanied by] five smaller boats, and chariots, and a large number of horses. And when this god had passed over to the place where Bent-Resht was, he worked upon the daughter of the Prince of Bekhten with his magical power, and she became better (i.e., was healed) straightway. And this spirit which had been with her said, in the presence of Khensu, [called] 'Pa-ari-sekher-em-Uast,' 'Come in peace, O great god, who dost drive away the spirits which attack! Bekhten is thy city, the people thereof, both men and women, are thy servants, and I myself am thy servant.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), the Bekhten legend.

passages.text: And [when] this god had tarried for three years and nine months in Bekhten, the Prince of Bekhten, who was lying down asleep on his bed, saw this god come forth outside his shrine (now he was in the form of a golden hawk), and he flew up into the heavens and departed to Egypt; and when the Prince woke up he was trembling. And he said unto the prophet of Khensu, [called] 'Pa-ari-sekher-em-Uast,' 'This god who tarried with us hath departed to Egypt; let his chariot also depart to Egypt.' And the Prince of Bekhten permitted [the image of] the god to set out for Egypt, and he gave him many great gifts of beautiful things of all kinds.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), the Bekhten legend, closing.

title.en: The Lamentations of Isis and Nephthys
title.zh: 伊西斯與奈芙蒂斯哀歌

region.en: Abydos, Upper Egypt (recited at the Osiris festival in the temple)
region.zh: 埃及上埃及阿拜多斯（奧西里斯祭期間於神廟誦唱）

texts.period: Recited on the 25th day of the 4th month of Akhet; Graeco-Roman copies of far older liturgy (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. V, 'The Lamentations of Isis and Nephthys' (Berlin papyrus)

summary.en: Two 'fair women' with the gods' names on their shoulders sang this alternately at the Osiris mysteries: Isis calls her murdered husband home — 'Come to thy house, come to thy house, O An... I am thy sister who loved thee upon earth; none other loved thee more' — and Nephthys joins her weeping, each verse a spell for the resurrection of Osiris and of the dead who hear it.
summary.zh: 肩佩神名的兩位『貞女』於奧西里斯祭中輪唱此歌：伊西斯召亡夫歸家——『歸家，歸家，安神……我乃世上愛你之姊，愛你者莫過於姊』；奈芙蒂斯泣而應和——每節皆為奧西里斯與聞者亡靈復活之咒。

sensitivity.note: Ancient ritual lament; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: ISIS SAITH: 'Come to thy house, come to thy house, O An, come to thy house. Thine enemy [Set] hath perished. O beautiful youth, come to thy house. Look thou upon me. I am the sister who loveth thee, go not far from me. O Beautiful Boy, come to thy house, straightway, straightway. I cannot see thee, and my heart weepeth for thee; my eyes follow thee about. I am following thee about so that I may see thee. Lo, I wait to see thee, I wait to see thee; behold, Prince, I wait to see thee. It is good to see thee, it is good to see thee; O An, it is good to see thee. Come to thy beloved one, come to thy beloved one, O Un-Nefer, whose word is truth.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. V, the Lamentations of Isis and Nephthys.

passages.text: Isis saith: 'Come to thy wife, O thou whose heart is still. Come to the lady of thy house; I am thy sister from thy mother's [womb]. Go not thou far from me. The faces of gods and men are turned towards thee, they all weep for thee together. As soon as I saw thee I cried out to thee, weeping with a loud voice which pierced the heavens, and thou didst not hear my voice. I am thy sister who loved thee upon earth; none other loved thee more than [thy] sister, thy sister.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Lamentations of Isis.

passages.text: NEPHTHYS SAITH: 'O Beautiful Prince, come to thy house. Let thy heart rejoice and be glad, for thine enemies have ceased to be. Thy two Sisters are nigh unto thee; they guard thy bier, they address thee with words [full of] tears as thou liest prone on thy bier. Look thou at the young women; speak to us, O our Sovereign Lord. Destroy thou all the misery that is in our hearts; the chiefs among gods and men look upon thee. Turn thou towards us thy face, O our Sovereign Lord. At the sight of thy face life cometh to our faces; turn not thou thy face from us. The joy of our heart is in the sight of thee. O Beautiful Sovereign, our hearts would see thee. I am thy sister Nephthys who loveth thee. The fiend Seba hath fallen, he hath not being. I am with thee, and I act as the protectress of thy members for ever and ever.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Lamentations of Nephthys.

passages.text: The rubric directs that the book were recited on behalf of any deceased person it would make his spirit to be glorious, and stablish his body, and cause his Ka to rejoice, and give breath to his nostrils and air to his throat. The two 'fair women' sang the sections alternately in the presence of the Kher-heb and Setem priests. One of these had the name of Isis on her shoulder, and the other the name of Nephthys, and each held a vessel of water in her right hand, and a 'Memphis cake of bread' in her left.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Budge (1910), ch. V rubric and performance directions; not verbatim.
